Dockflow

Making the next dock assignment easier to understand.

My role
Product direction & AI-assisted implementation
Focus
Operations decision support
Built with
React & TypeScript

The operational question

An urgent trailer cannot simply go to the next available door. Placement also depends on physical occupancy, handling requirements, destination compatibility, and how current the load information is. I wanted to make those constraints visible in the same place as the priority decision.

My contribution

I defined an independent demonstration of this workflow and used AI coding assistance to build and publish it while developing my technical skills. Dockflow combines a deadline-based queue, destination-demand heatmap, door plan, and exception list using fictional facility data.

A user selects a trailer, inspects the proposed door or its blocking reason, and approves a simulated assignment. They can choose another eligible door with an explanation, inspect decision history, and undo an action. Repeatable scenarios make different operating conditions easy to explore.

The rules behind the recommendation

Urgency determines the order of consideration. Every proposal must still satisfy occupancy, handling, destination, and freshness requirements. A held trailer continues to occupy its door. Missing profile data stays missing. Accepting a proposal checks the current state again, so an earlier recommendation cannot silently override a changed condition.

The application runs in the browser and preserves a visitor’s work locally. It demonstrates the decision process without requiring warehouse access or connecting to live dispatch systems.

Evidence and next steps

The verification record includes 24 behavioral tests, type checking, a production build, and browser checks of assignment, recovery, and persistence. These establish simulator behavior, not warehouse productivity gains. The next evaluation would test whether operators understand recommendations, recognize blocked loads, and recover from mistakes.
